prompt: A function that is both one-one and onto is called:
explanation: One-one is INJECTIVE, onto is SURJECTIVE, and both together is BIJECTIVE. The bi is the clue: two properties at once. A bijection pairs every input with exactly one output and leaves nothing in the codomain unused, which is why it is the only kind that has an inverse.

why.a: Correct. Injective and surjective together.
why.b: Wrong. A constant function sends everything to one value, so it is as far from one-one as possible.
why.c: Wrong. Many-one means two inputs share an output, which breaks one-one.
why.d: Wrong. Into means the codomain has spare elements, which breaks onto.

prompt: Proof where conclusion already known true:
explanation: Two odd-looking proofs come as a pair and the exam asks for both. TRIVIAL: the conclusion q is already true, so p implies q holds whatever p does. VACUOUS: the hypothesis p is false, so the implication holds whatever q does. Trivial leans on the conclusion; vacuous leans on the hypothesis.

why.a: Correct. The conclusion is already true, so the implication cannot fail.
why.b: Wrong. Proof by cases splits the problem into exhaustive possibilities.
why.c: Wrong. Contrapositive proves not-q implies not-p instead.
why.d: Wrong. Contradiction assumes the opposite and derives an impossibility.

prompt: GP terms are obtained by:
explanation: GP MULTIPLIES by a fixed ratio r, so 2, 6, 18, 54 with r = 3. AP ADDS a fixed difference d, so 2, 4, 6, 8 with d = 2. The pair is the whole of this module: Add for Arithmetic, and the other one multiplies. Their nth terms follow: AP is a + (n-1)d, GP is ar to the power n-1.

why.a: Wrong. Squaring each term is not a progression of either kind.
why.b: Wrong, and that is the ARITHMETIC progression.
why.c: Wrong, and impossible: division by zero is undefined.
why.d: Correct. A constant ratio, multiplied each time.

prompt: A function is onto if:

options.text: Every element of the codomain has at least one pre-image
Every element of the domain has two images

explanation: Onto, or SURJECTIVE, means nothing in the codomain is left out: every possible output is actually hit by something. Said the short way, the range EQUALS the codomain. Watch the wrong option that says domain equals range, which swaps the wrong two sets.

why.a: Wrong. Two pre-images each is not required, and would break one-one.
why.b: Wrong, and it is the trap: onto means RANGE equals CODOMAIN, not domain equals range.
why.c: Correct. Nothing in the codomain is missed.
why.d: Wrong, and impossible: a function gives each input exactly ONE output.

prompt: A function in which different elements of the domain have different images is called:
explanation: Different in, different out: no two inputs ever collide on the same output. That is ONE-ONE, or injective. Its opposite is many-one, where several inputs land on the same image. The everyday test: if you can find two inputs with the same output, it is not injective.

why.a: Wrong. Constant sends everything to one output, the extreme of many-one.
why.b: Wrong, and it is the exact opposite: many-one lets inputs share an image.
why.c: Correct. Different elements have different images.
why.d: Wrong. Into is about the codomain having spare elements, which is the onto question rather than the one-one one.

prompt: Proof relying on false hypothesis:
explanation: VACUOUS: p is false, so p implies q is automatically true. Every unicorn in this room is purple is vacuously true, because there are no unicorns. It is the partner of the trivial proof two questions back: vacuous leans on a false HYPOTHESIS, trivial on a true CONCLUSION.

why.a: Wrong. Cases splits into exhaustive alternatives and proves each.
why.b: Wrong. Direct proof assumes the hypothesis is TRUE and reasons forward.
why.c: Correct. The hypothesis is false, so the implication holds regardless.
why.d: Wrong. Induction proves a statement for all natural numbers by base case and step.

prompt: Which statement about function composition is correct?

options.text: f of g is not equal to g of f in general

explanation: Order matters. Take f(x) = x + 1 and g(x) = 2x. Then f of g gives 2x + 1, while g of f gives 2x + 2. Different functions. Composition is ASSOCIATIVE but not COMMUTATIVE, exactly like putting on socks and shoes: the order changes the outcome.

why.a: Correct. They differ in general, and one counterexample settles it.
why.b: Wrong. Composition is perfectly possible whenever the range of the inner function fits the domain of the outer.
why.c: Wrong. Identical would mean order never matters, and it does.
why.d: Wrong for the same reason: equality holds only in special cases, not generally.

prompt: The set of all allowable outputs of a function is called the:
explanation: Three sets, and this module keeps swapping between them. DOMAIN is what goes in. CODOMAIN is what is ALLOWED to come out. RANGE is what ACTUALLY comes out. The hook: codomain is the whole target board, range is where the darts actually landed, and onto is when they cover the board.

why.a: Wrong. An image is one particular output, of one particular input.
why.b: Correct. The declared set of allowable outputs.
why.c: Wrong. The domain is the set of inputs.
why.d: Wrong, and this is the trap: the range is what is actually reached, which may be smaller.

prompt: After assuming P(k):
explanation: Induction has exactly two moves. BASE CASE: show P(1) is true. INDUCTIVE STEP: assume P(k), then prove P(k+1). Always forward by one. The assumption is called the inductive hypothesis, and using it is the whole point rather than cheating.

why.a: Wrong direction. Induction climbs upward, not down.
why.b: Wrong. Nothing restarts; the step is what carries you along the whole chain.
why.c: Correct. From k to k plus 1.
why.d: Wrong. Doubling is a different technique and not standard induction.

prompt: A function in which two or more elements of the domain have the same image is called:
explanation: MANY inputs to ONE output, so many-one. f(x) = x squared is the standard case: 2 and -2 both give 4. It is the exact negation of one-one, which is why a function cannot be both, and why a many-one function can never have an inverse.

why.a: Wrong. Onto is about covering the codomain, a different property.
why.b: Wrong. Bijective requires one-one, which this breaks.
why.c: Wrong, and it is the opposite: one-one forbids shared images.
why.d: Correct. Several inputs share an image.

prompt: Direct proof begins by:
explanation: Direct proof takes p as given and reasons forward to q. Compare the three openings and the whole module falls into place: DIRECT assumes p true, CONTRAPOSITIVE assumes not-q and derives not-p, CONTRADICTION assumes p true AND q false and derives an impossibility.

why.a: Correct. Assume the hypothesis, reason forward to the conclusion.
why.b: Wrong. Assuming the conclusion false is where contradiction or contrapositive starts.
why.c: Wrong. The hypothesis is exactly what you are given to work with.
why.d: Wrong. That describes no standard technique.

prompt: A function is defined as a rule that assigns:
explanation: EXACTLY ONE output per input. That single phrase is what separates a function from a general relation, and it is why the vertical line test works on a graph. Many inputs may share an output, which is allowed and is called many-one, but one input may never have two outputs.

why.a: Wrong. Every element of the domain must get an output.
why.b: Correct. Each input gets exactly one output.
why.c: Wrong. That is a relation in general, not a function.
why.d: Wrong, and it is the one thing a function may never do.

prompt: First induction step:
explanation: The base case comes FIRST, usually P(1). Without it the whole chain has nothing to stand on: you could prove that if P(k) then P(k+1) for a statement that is never true at all, and prove nothing. Base case first, inductive step second, and marks are given for both.

why.a: Correct. Verify the base case, usually P(1).
why.b: Wrong. Derivatives belong to calculus, not to induction.
why.c: Wrong. Assuming something false is contradiction, a different technique.
why.d: Wrong. The step goes to k plus 1, and it comes second in any case.

prompt: The sequence 2, 4, 6, 8, ... is:
explanation: Subtract consecutive terms: 4 minus 2 is 2, 6 minus 4 is 2, 8 minus 6 is 2. A constant DIFFERENCE, so arithmetic, with d = 2. Test any sequence the same way: subtract for a common difference, divide for a common ratio. Whichever comes out constant names the progression.

why.a: Correct. A common difference of 2.
why.b: Wrong. Fibonacci adds the two previous terms, giving 1, 1, 2, 3, 5.
why.c: Wrong. Dividing gives 2, 1.5, 1.33, which is not constant.
why.d: Wrong. A harmonic sequence is the reciprocals of an arithmetic one.

prompt: Domino analogy means:

options.text: Base case and each step implies next so all hold

explanation: A row of dominoes needs two things to all fall: you must PUSH the first one, and each must be close enough to knock over the next. Push the first is the base case; each knocks the next is the inductive step. Miss either and nothing falls, which is exactly why both halves earn marks.

why.a: Wrong. Contradiction is a separate technique and not what the analogy shows.
why.b: Correct. The first falls, each knocks over the next, so all fall.
why.c: Wrong, and far too loose to be a statement about induction.
why.d: Wrong. Theorems are proved; conjectures are not.

prompt: Which is Fibonacci?
explanation: Each term is the SUM OF THE TWO BEFORE IT: 1 + 1 = 2, 1 + 2 = 3, 2 + 3 = 5, 3 + 5 = 8. That makes it a recurrence relation rather than a progression, which is why it reappears in Module Twelve as F(n) = F(n-1) + F(n-2).

why.a: Wrong. That is arithmetic, with a common difference of 5.
why.b: Wrong. Arithmetic again, difference 2.
why.c: Wrong. Geometric, with a ratio of 3.
why.d: Correct. Each term is the sum of the previous two.

prompt: A sequence with fixed number of terms is:
explanation: Fixed number of terms means it stops, so it is finite. An infinite sequence goes on without end. The distinction matters when a question asks for a SUM: a finite arithmetic series has the formula n over 2, times first plus last, while an infinite geometric series only has a sum at all when the ratio is between minus one and one.

why.a: Correct. A fixed, countable number of terms.
why.b: Wrong, although a sequence IS a kind of function, which is the next question.
why.c: Wrong. A recurrence defines terms from earlier ones; it says nothing about how many.
why.d: Wrong, and the opposite.

prompt: A helping theorem is a:
explanation: Four words in one family, and the exam asks for all four. LEMMA: a small result proved to help prove a bigger one, so it comes BEFORE. COROLLARY: a result that follows easily from one just proved, so it comes AFTER. THEOREM: a major proved statement. CONJECTURE: believed true but not yet proved. Lemma before, corollary after.

why.a: Wrong. A hypothesis is what you assume, not something proved.
why.b: Correct. A helper proved on the way to the main theorem.
why.c: Wrong. A corollary follows AFTER the theorem, as a consequence.
why.d: Wrong. A proposition is a statement, usually a lesser theorem, not specifically a helper.

prompt: A sequence is:

options.text: A function from a subset of integers to a set

explanation: Formally a sequence is a FUNCTION whose domain is a subset of the integers, usually 1, 2, 3 and onwards. So the third term is just the value of that function at 3. Reading it this way explains the notation a-sub-n, and it explains why order matters: the input decides the position.

why.a: Wrong. A matrix is a rectangular array, a different object.
why.b: Wrong, and inverted: the integers are the INPUT, not the output.
why.c: Correct. A function from a subset of the integers into a set.
why.d: Wrong. A sequence is ordered, and that is its defining feature.

prompt: A proved formal statement is a:
explanation: PROVED is the word that decides it. A theorem has a proof; a conjecture does not yet. A definition assigns a meaning and needs no proof at all, and an assumption is granted rather than shown. Sort them by whether a proof exists: theorem yes, conjecture not yet, definition and assumption not applicable.

why.a: Wrong. A definition assigns meaning; there is nothing to prove.
why.b: Wrong. An assumption is taken for granted, the opposite of proved.
why.c: Correct. A formal statement that has been proved.
why.d: Wrong. A conjecture is believed but unproved, which is the next question.

prompt: The set of all possible inputs of a function is called the:
explanation: Domain in, codomain and range out. Say it as a sentence you can repeat under pressure: the DOMAIN is everything allowed IN, the CODOMAIN is everything allowed OUT, the RANGE is what actually comes out. Three of the thirty questions on this paper turn on nothing but that sentence.

why.a: Wrong. The codomain is on the output side.
why.b: Wrong. An image is a single output value.
why.c: Wrong. The range is the set of outputs actually achieved.
why.d: Correct. The set of all permitted inputs.

prompt: The inverse of a function exists only when the function is:
explanation: Both properties are needed, and each fails for its own reason. If it is NOT one-one, two inputs share an output and the inverse would not know which to return. If it is NOT onto, some codomain element has no input at all and the inverse would be undefined there. Only a bijection escapes both, which is why bijective and invertible mean the same thing.

why.a: Wrong. A constant function sends everything to one value, so it is as far from invertible as possible.
why.b: Wrong. Many-one is exactly the case where the inverse cannot choose.
why.c: Correct. One-one and onto together.
why.d: Wrong. Into means not onto, so part of the codomain has nothing mapping to it.

prompt: Total number of functions from a set X with m elements to a set Y with n elements:
explanation: Reason it out rather than memorising. Each of the m inputs must be sent somewhere, and each has n choices, independently. Multiply n by itself m times: n to the power m. Sanity-check it on tiny numbers: 2 inputs into 3 outputs gives 3 squared, which is 9, and you can list all nine. That check also tells you instantly which way round the letters go.

why.a: Correct. Each of the m inputs has n choices, so n to the power m.
why.b: Wrong. m times n counts the PAIRS, that is the Cartesian product, not the functions.
why.c: Wrong. Adding has no meaning here.
why.d: Wrong, and it is the trap: the letters are the wrong way round. Test it on 2 into 3 and you get 8 rather than 9.

prompt: An unproved likely true statement:
explanation: UNPROVED is the deciding word. A conjecture is believed on evidence but not yet demonstrated, and it becomes a theorem the moment somebody proves it. Goldbach's conjecture is the famous example: checked for enormous numbers, still unproved.

why.a: Wrong. A lemma is proved, and proved in order to help prove something else.
why.b: Wrong. A theorem is proved, which is precisely what this is not.
why.c: Correct. Believed true, not yet proved.
why.d: Wrong. A corollary is proved, as an easy consequence of a theorem.

prompt: A recurrence relation expresses:
explanation: A recurrence defines each term from the ones before it, which is why it always needs INITIAL CONDITIONS to get started. F(n) = F(n-1) + F(n-2) with F(1) = F(2) = 1 is Fibonacci. Without the starting values the rule describes infinitely many different sequences.

why.a: Wrong. It gives a rule for terms in general, not just the last one.
why.b: Wrong, and it is the opposite: an explicit formula gives terms independently, a recurrence does not.
why.c: Correct. Each term is defined from earlier ones.
why.d: Wrong. The first term is the initial CONDITION, which the recurrence needs but is not.

prompt: The composition of two functions g and f is written as:
explanation: Composition is a substitution, not an arithmetic operation: apply f first, then feed the result into g. The notation reads RIGHT TO LEFT, which catches almost everyone. g composed with f means g of f of x, so f goes first even though it is written second.

why.a: Correct. Apply f, then g, written g of f of x.
why.b: Wrong. That is arithmetic on the outputs, not composition.
why.c: Wrong. Adding two functions is a different operation entirely.
why.d: Wrong. That adds a variable to a function, which is not composition.

prompt: An integer of the form 2k is:
explanation: 2k is two times a whole number, so it is EVEN by definition, and 2k + 1 is odd. These two forms are the working parts of half the proofs in this module: to prove something about an even number you write it as 2k and manipulate, which is exactly how the classic proof that the sum of two evens is even goes.

why.a: Wrong. Odd numbers are 2k plus 1.
why.b: Wrong. The only even prime is 2 itself; 2k is composite for k greater than 1.
why.c: Wrong. All integers are rational, so this distinguishes nothing.
why.d: Correct. Twice an integer is even, by definition.

prompt: The range of a function is:

options.text: The set of all images of elements in the domain
The same as the domain in every function

explanation: The range is what ACTUALLY comes out: every image of every element of the domain, and nothing else. It is always a subset of the codomain, and the two are equal exactly when the function is ONTO. That sentence links this question to question 4 on the same paper.

why.a: Correct. All the images of the domain's elements.
why.b: Wrong. Domain and range are different sets except by coincidence.
why.c: Wrong. Pre-images are on the INPUT side; that describes the domain.
why.d: Wrong. The range depends on the function, and need not involve integers at all.

prompt: If f(a) = b, then b is called the:
explanation: b is what a MAPS TO, so b is the image of a, and a is the pre-image of b. Keep the direction straight with the prefix: PRE means before, so the pre-image comes before the arrow and the image after it. The wrong options here are all sets rather than elements, which is a second way to spot them.

why.a: Wrong. The domain is a whole set of inputs, not a single output.
why.b: Correct. b is the image of a.
why.c: Wrong. The codomain is a set, and it is not attached to a single element.
why.d: Wrong, and exactly reversed: a is the pre-image of b.

prompt: The difference between consecutive AP terms is called:
explanation: AP has a common DIFFERENCE d, found by subtracting. GP has a common RATIO r, found by dividing. The words match the operation, so if you remember that arithmetic adds and geometric multiplies, both names follow. In 2, 4, 6, 8 the common difference is 2.

why.a: Wrong. No such term is used.
why.b: Wrong, and it belongs to the GEOMETRIC progression.
why.c: Correct. The constant amount added each time.
why.d: Wrong. Gradient is the slope of a line, and although an AP plots as a straight line, the term used here is common difference.
